scene_start: Afternoon on Polmarren harbour. Old Jack is mending nets when Sam, down from London, stops to say hello.
beats: Sam asks how Jack mends a net; Jack shows him a knot.
Jack asks why Sam has come down here on his own.
Jack invites Sam out on the boat tomorrow morning.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam asks how Jack mends a net; Jack shows him a knot. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Blimey, you've got your hands absolutely covered in twine, mate; how do you even manage to keep all those knots tight without any kind of automated loom or something? It looks proper analogue, but kinda fascinating to watch.

speaker: lao
text: Aye, lad, it's just the knot and the hands, nothing fancy like that. My old bones remember tying lines tougher than any rope you've seen in your time. I learned it from me father, and before him too, up on the trawlers when the sea was running rough. You just take yer time and keep yer eyes on the twine.

speaker: minh
text: Right, so it's all muscle memory then, no fancy algorithms needed, that's proper old school. Do you ever use any kind of sort of tracking system for where you've already mended, or is it purely visual estimation?

speaker: lao
text: Tracking it? No, boy, I just know the harbour by heart, like the lines of this tide. Me eyes have seen more fish come and go than any chart you've got. When I was out off Iceland, you learned to judge the depth by the swell, not by some blinking box. You'll get the hang of it yourself, I reckon.

speaker: minh
text: Blimey, Iceland, that sounds epic; so you’re basically running on pure data points from experience, like a massive, biological dataset. When the weather gets really rough, do you ever have to adjust your whole operational flow, or is it just reactive?

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack asks why Sam has come down here on his own. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: When the gale hits, lad, you stop thinking and you start *feeling* the boat pitch and roll. You just learn to ride the rhythm of it, like a good sea can teach you. Tell me though, lad, you're all the way down from London, aren't ye? What brings a young man like yourself down to Polmarren these days?

speaker: minh
text: Yeah, just on leave from work, mate; the whole software grind got a bit much, you know? It’s just nice to get away from the screens and see something that hasn't been optimized or containerised. You reckon the sea's vibe is a proper natural anti-burnout patch, or what?

speaker: lao
text: Nonsense talk about screens and all that; the sea just *is*, lad, it doesn't need patchin' up. The salt spray and the smell of diesel, that'll settle a man's spirit quicker than any bit of rest. You look like a lad who spends too much time looking at things that aren't actually there. You enjoying the quiet, are ye, boy?

speaker: minh
text: Nah, I'm just trying to switch off the background noise, you know? It’s just different from the usual city hum, for sure. It's proper grounding, seeing things that aren't running on some cloud server.

speaker: lao
text: Well, the city hum, ye say? Sounds like a racket to me, lad, nothing like the sound of the wind whistling through the rigging. My son, he writes from Plymouth sometimes, says the sea air does a man good, but he never stood here mending nets himself. You'll find the rhythm of the tide beats louder than any city noise. You'll get used to the proper sound of it, I promise ye.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack invites Sam out on the boat tomorrow morning. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Crikey, you've got a bit of a philosopher in you, Jack, talking about rhythms and vibes. If you're out on the boat tomorrow, I reckon I might actually give this 'natural data input' a whirl, just to see what the output is like. You think it'll be worth the trip out?

speaker: lao
text: The sea'll show ye what it wants to show ye, lad, that's all there is to it. Don't go out 'cause you think you must, go out 'cause the nets are waiting for mendin'. We'll be heading out with the tide turning early, catching some mackerel if the wind holds. You'd better be up before the sun gets too high, or you'll just be gawking at the foam.

speaker: minh
text: Right, mashing up with the local experts on mackerel runs, I get it. So, if the wind's holding, is the mackerel usually concentrated near the shallows, or are they more of a deep-water pattern? Sounds like a proper plan for a few hours, Jack.

speaker: lao
text: The mackerel can be anywhere, boy, depends on the currents playing tricks on 'em. When it's running deep, you have to follow the eddies, near where the old oyster beds used to be. You'll see the puffmarks on the water before you smell 'em, I'll wager. You've got a keen eye for this, lad, better than you look like.

speaker: minh
text: Puffmarks, right, so it’s like reading the residual signal strength on a water surface, I guess. Do you ever use any sort of local knowledge database, like an analogue map, to predict where those eddies might pop up in different conditions?

speaker: lao
text: We use the colour of the water and where the kelp breaks up, lad, that's the map we read. My gut tells me where the current will fight hardest, and fish love a fight, aye. You keep your eyes peeled for the way the water breaks just before it hits the sand. You'll see more in an hour on this tide than you've seen in all your fancy books.

speaker: minh
text: It sounds like you've got a whole suite of environmental variables you're tracking manually, which is seriously impressive processing power. I might have to take notes on your methodology; it's a whole different kind of system architecture than anything I've ever dealt with. Cheers for the tips, Jack.

speaker: lao
text: You're taking notes, are ye, lad, like some scholar after a rare catch? Best ye just keep yer eyes on the water for now, it'll teach ye better than any book. My old fingers have seen enough storms and enough hauls to know when the fish are hiding. Now, if ye'll excuse me, I reckon there's a good stretch of net waiting for a proper mend.

summary: Jack taught Sam that he learned his knot-tying skills from his father and through years working on trawlers, and that he predicts fish location by reading the color of the water and where the kelp breaks up. Sam revealed he came to Polmarren from London on leave from work, and Jack mentioned that his son writes from Plymouth.

scene_start: Next morning, still dark, Sam goes out with Old Jack in his small boat.
beats: Sam gets seasick and Jack shows him how to ride it out.
Shooting the nets, Jack explains the tides and the fishing seasons.
They haul up a strange fish and argue about what it is.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam gets seasick and Jack shows him how to ride it out. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Hold fast now, lad, don't fight the swell like that. Just breathe with the rhythm of the tide, like you're breathing yourself. When I was your age, out on the trawler, I felt the same way, but you just had to let the boat take you where it wills. Soon enough, this rolling will pass us by.

speaker: minh
text: Blimey, the sea's proper rough, isn't it? I wish I could just film this, but my phone's completely dead, which is proper rubbish. You reckon reading the swell is like an algorithmic pattern recognition, or is it just pure instinct?

speaker: lao
text: Kernalf, lad, you wouldn't know an algorhythm from a seaweed tangle. Instinct is what it is, pure and simple, like knowing when the cod will bite. I remember being just fourteen, out on a trawler, and the water told me where the silver run was, no clever box could tell that. Just watch the way the kelp breaks up, boy, that's all there is to it.

speaker: minh
text: Yeah, no fancy GPS needed, I get it, though I'm used to things being quantifiable, you know? It's wild thinking about how much you learned just by being out here day in and day out. So, what's the best bit of gear you'd recommend for spotting those fish without needing any sort of bio-sensor?

speaker: lao
text: Lad, you don't need no fancy bits to see a good haul. When I was your age, I used to just watch the gulls circle over the patch where the water looked darkest. I remember the first time I spotted a decent school, just by the way the little bits of foam caught the morning sun. Keep yer eyes peeled, boy, and yer gut will tell you when the good fish are thick beneath the waves.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Shooting the nets, Jack explains the tides and the fishing seasons. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Right, so the gulls are basically your early warning system, I suppose—quite the natural data feed! When you've been fishing this long, are there certain times of year where the whole system changes, like a major seasonal update? I'm trying to picture how the tides influence everything, almost like a predictable cyclical function.

speaker: lao
text: Aye, the seasons change the whole bloody slate, lad, you'll learn that with time. When I was just fourteen, the summer was a right mystery, the sea behaving like a girl's temper. The best time, mind you, is when the tide's turning with a steady push, not a wild tug-of-war. Just keep yer eyes on the colour of the water near the drop-off, that'll tell you more than any fancy clock.

speaker: minh
text: So, basically the tide's *state* is the key variable, not just the time itself? It's funny, I feel like I need to document this whole thing for some kind of portfolio piece, but my phone's completely dead, which is proper annoying. If you had to program a simple model to predict the best fishing spot based only on colour gradients and tidal flow, what parameters would you tell me to focus on first?

speaker: lao
text: Blast it all, lad, you and your notions of programming and models. When I was just fourteen, I didn't know a thing of that nonsense, I just saw the water turning a deep, oily green near the reef that day. I remember seeing a school of mackerel burst out, bright as shillings, right where the tide was slowing down against the rocks. Focus on where the current slackens, boy, and keep yer nets ready.

speaker: minh
text: Bloody hell, mackerel bursting out like shillings, that's a proper visual, I could practically see it pop up. It sounds like the area where the current is slowing down is the prime zone, like a natural bottleneck in the system. I really wish I could snap a pic of this spot right now to properly map it out.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: They haul up a strange fish and argue about what it is. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Look at this mess, lad, what in the devil's name is this catch? It ain't no cod, nor is it haddock, look at yer father's net. When I was about your age, out on the deep, I pulled up a thing that looked like a mermaid's tail, and no one knew a soul what it was. It’s a strange one, this beast, smells of the deep bottom where the light never reaches.

speaker: minh
text: Blimey, what *is* that thing, Jack? It looks completely alien; I'd never even know how to classify that in any database. I'm gutted 'cause I can't film this, but honestly, this is way more interesting than any piece of code I've written lately.

speaker: lao
text: Never seen such a thing, lad, it smells of depths no man ought to wander to. When I first pulled up a haul like this, I was barely fourteen, and my stomach dropped right into my boots. It was a time the sea showed me what it kept hidden from the sun, a proper humbling sight. Just keep the boat pointed where the water looks deepest, boy, and leave the rest to the tide.

speaker: minh
text: Crikey, that is genuinely bizarre; it’s like finding some undocumented species in a whole new ecological zone. I'm gutted because I can't get a proper shot of this thing, it's such a massive content failure. Still, I'll take your word for it, Jack; I'll keep the boat pointed towards the deepest bits, even if I have to rely on pure instinct.

speaker: lao
text: Remember that feeling, lad, when the sea shows you a secret like that. I first saw a thing like this near the Lizard, when I was just fourteen, felt like I was looking at the bottom of the world. You learn quick enough that the sea keeps its best wonders hidden, only showing 'em to a man who knows how to wait for it. Now, let's haul these lines in before the sun climbs too high.

speaker: minh
text: Right, let's get this haul secured, I guess, even if I can't post about it later. It's mad thinking about how much of this stuff is undocumented knowledge, totally off the grid from any scientific journal, you know? Hopefully, I can still get a decent angle of this weird catch before we have to motor back to shore.

speaker: lao
text: Just get the lines stacked neat, lad, before the tide turns against us. When I first saw a haul like this, I was barely fourteen, and my stomach dropped right into my boots. It was a time the sea showed me what it kept hidden from the sun, a proper humbling sight. Now, let's get the boat pointed back towards Polmarren before the afternoon haze settles in.

event: A boat comes alongside and someone shouts: "Jack! Give us a hand with these nets!"

speaker: minh
text: Blimey, look at that boat pulling up; looks like we're part of some kind of maritime documentary, eh? I'd kill for a decent shot of this whole chaotic scene, but my phone's still bricked, which is proper rubbish timing. Right then, Jack, let's get these lines stacked up like you said before we have to navigate back to Polmarren.

summary: Sam and Old Jack were on a small boat when a third boat arrived, prompting Sam to note their location was near Polmarren. Jack learned that Sam was interested in quantifying natural patterns, while Sam learned Jack had seen strange deep-sea objects when he was only fourteen years old.

scene_start: Midday on the quay, Old Jack sells his catch and Sam lends a hand.
goal: A morning at the fish stall.
beats: A customer haggles hard over the price.
Sam gets the change wrong and Jack laughs it off.
The woman at the next stall teases Sam about being Jack's new son-in-law.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: A customer haggles hard over the price. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: So, you reckon we could maybe list some of this on one of those online marketplaces? Like, a whole digital inventory, you know? It might take the guesswork out of the haggling a bit.

speaker: lao
text: Blast it, lad, I know nothing of your online marketplaces or your digital lists. I've seen young Thomas down at the bait shop and old Mr. Parris mending nets by the slipway, and they know their prices good. My catch today's worth a decent few shillings, enough for a proper supper at the pub. You'll see the lads on the quay sorted out enough without no fancy counting.

speaker: minh
text: Right, yeah, I get it, it's a bit different from the London scene, innit? Still, if we could even get a basic dataset on the usual going rate, it'd be a bit more predictable than just eyeballing it, you know? Maybe some kind of basic algorithm could predict the best time to sell, even.

speaker: lao
text: You'll find the rhythm of this quay is older than any of your fancy reckoning, lad. Old Man Hemlock always sells his best haddock right when the tide turns, and I know it by the look in his eye. Maureen down the way always gets the best price for her crab pot haul, no matter what you calculate. Just watch the men, boy; they know the water and the buying from years of doing the same thing.

speaker: minh
text: Yeah, I get the whole 'reading the vibe' thing, I really do. But even the best human intuition can be biased, right? If we could just model out the variables for price fluctuations, maybe it would cut down on the guesswork even for the lads.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Sam gets the change wrong and Jack laughs it off. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Now hold on a minute, lad, you and your guessing games. You'll learn that watching my neighbour, Tom, haggle with the fishmonger is a better lesson than any book. He'll get it wrong half the time, but he'll get it right enough for a good laugh. You'll see it when you count out your change, I reckon you'll need a bit of help with the shillings anyway.

speaker: minh
text: Nah, don't worry about the change, I'm alright with counting bits and bobs, I'm used to debugging massive amounts of code. It's just... it feels like there's a missing data layer here, like we're missing the whole 'e-commerce' function to this whole operation. Maybe we could just cobble together a simple little webpage for it?

speaker: lao
text: A webpage, you say? Sounds like something from a fancy Plymouth office, not this working quay. You see that old woman, Mrs. Davies, she always knows who's buying the best mackerel before anyone else even opens their mouth. And young Billy, he'll trade a handful of his bright shells for anything worthwhile, you'll see that when the tide runs out. Now, if you want to earn your keep, help me haul these creels before the sun gets too high.

speaker: minh
text: Right, yeah, the creels, got it, I can help with that instead of talking about servers. It’s just, it’s weird not being able to just ping some info out to someone instantly, you know? Still, hauling gear sounds way less abstract than data structuring, so I'm game for that.

speaker: lao
text: Aye, that'll do, lad, a bit of honest backache'll do you good. See that fellow by the lobster pots, that's Davey's boy, always mending those ropes like he's got the measure of the sea in his hands. Over there, Mr. Parris is sorting his gear; he'll trade you a good story for a clean knot on your lines. Pull on this one, boy, it's got a good weight to it, just like a proper catch.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: The woman at the next stall teases Sam about being Jack's new son-in-law. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Blimey, I'm knackered already, but pulling these things is actually kinda grounding, I'll admit. Speaking of things being sorted, you know, seeing all this effort, it does make me wonder if there’s a way to streamline the sales process digitally, even just for tracking what sells best. Anyway, what's that woman over there saying about me?

speaker: lao
text: Now stop your worrying about what folks are whispering, lad; they'll talk about everything from the wind to the weeds growing on the tide line. That old curmudgeon, Mr. Parris, he's just telling Maureen that you've got the hands of a dock worker, not a London tourist. And young Tommy, he's nodding along, saying you've got a good bit of grit, which is more than some folks bring to the boat. Now heave, lad, let's get these last few creels stacked up before the afternoon drift sets in.

speaker: minh
text: Honestly, I appreciate the morale boost, Mr Penrose, but I'm still kinda preoccupied with this whole sales angle. It's just that, even if it's a massive stretch, thinking about how we could get this stuff seen beyond just the quay feels like a puzzle I need to solve. Maybe I could sketch out a very basic wireframe idea later, if you don't mind.

speaker: lao
text: Lad, you'll get your cobbling in Plymouth, I'll wager, but down here we use our eyes and our guts, not your sketches. Just look at old Mr. Parris over there; he knows every buyer from here to St Ives by the look on their faces. And see poor little Davey's boy, he can mend a net blindfolded, which is worth more than all your fancy plans. Now, get your hands on these ropes, they're stiff with salt, boy.

speaker: minh
text: Right, I'm getting the message, Jack, it's all about the local vibe and reading people, I get it. But even if we just took photos of the best hauls and uploaded them somewhere, like a simple gallery, wouldn't that give us a bit of an edge? It'd be like having a pre-loaded catalog for potential buyers.

speaker: lao
text: A photo gallery, you say? I'd trust a good pair of weathered eyes more than any looking glass, lad. You see that stout fellow, Mr. Gideon, he'll buy a dozen pounds of crab just by knowing his name. And Maureen, she'll take a picture of her haul, sure, but she'll know who to show it to face to face. Now enough of this talking, boy; help me haul these last few pots, they're heavy enough to take a man's breath.

speaker: minh
text: Bloody hell, my arms are killing me, but yeah, I'm with you on the pots, Jack. Still, it’s just so strange not being able to ping a picture of this haul straight onto a cloud drive for later viewing, you know? I think I'll just stick to hauling for now, though.

speaker: lao
text: Aye, your arms will thank you when the tide turns and you're sitting down with a pint. That little cloud nonsense of yours won't keep a hungry belly full, boy. You see that lass near the fish stalls, she's got a shawl the colour of the deep sea, and over by the bait shop, little Tommy's playing with a bit of driftwood, he's got the eyes of a proper sailor. Now, mind where you step, the tide's pulling strong out by the pilings.

summary: Sam suggested using online marketplaces and digital datasets to predict sales, while Jack pointed out that local knowledge, such as that held by Mr. Parris and Maureen, is more valuable. They learned names like Old Jack, Sam, Mr. Parris, Maureen, Thomas, Mrs. Davies, Billy, Mr. Gideon, and Tommy, along with details about their daily activities and local commerce.

scene_start: Evening, a storm is coming in; Sam runs down to help Jack haul the boat up the slipway.
beats: A gust hits and the mooring rope slips.
Jack talks about the Great Storm of 1987.
The boat is safe and they run to Jack's cottage out of the rain.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: A gust hits and the mooring rope slips. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Steady now, lad, hold tight to that rope, the wind's picking up proper. Reckon this tide'll be a right beast by morning, much like the one in eighty-seven. I remember young Tom out there that day, never saw him again near the shoals. Mind how the wave hits you, lad, or you'll be wrestling with the sea.

speaker: minh
text: Blimey, this is proper intense, Jack; I've never seen anything like this weather, it's seriously messing with my equilibrium. You reckon the structural integrity of the slipway can handle this, or are we gonna have some kind of system crash? Hope my phone battery's got enough juice for some emergency geo-tagging if things get dicey.

speaker: lao
text: Hold fast now, boy, and keep your eyes on what's right in front of you. This old slipway’s seen worse weather than any fancy machine can measure, it'll hold its shape. We'll get the boat hauled up, just like we always do, mind you. It reminds me a bit of the night back in '87, when the sea took a man right off the deck near the headland.

speaker: minh
text: Crikey, that's proper grim, Jack; the sheer force of this water is seriously overwhelming, it’s almost like a rogue variable in a simulation. I've only seen weather forecasts, not actual maelstroms, so this is genuinely quite something. Do you think there's any way to model the current stress load on this wood, or is it purely empirical knowledge?

speaker: lao
text: Steady lad, don't you go thinking you can measure the sea with your fancy notions. This knowledge, it comes from grit and muscle, seeing enough waves crash over years. I recall that wild night in eighty-seven, the way the water moved when you least expected it, and there’s no book for that. Just keep pulling, boy, and keep your wits about you.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack talks about the Great Storm of 1987. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Right, I get it, Jack, the analogue data is king, I guess, but still, it's pretty staggering seeing this scale of power up close. When you talk about that '87 storm, are there specific patterns in the wave action from that night that you think are predictable, almost like a deep-sea algorithm? I'm just trying to map out any repeatable physics behind it all.

speaker: lao
text: The sea don't run on algorithms, lad, it runs on temper and wind. I remember the black water that night, the way it swallowed the light near the old Devil's Teeth. I lost poor Billy to that swell, didn't see him bobbing back to us. You learn to read the turning of the kelp, and that's all you ever need to know.

speaker: minh
text: Blimey, Jack, this is proper terrifying; I've never seen anything like this, it's properly sending my whole system into overload. So, it's just about reading the kelp, like a natural index of the water's mood, is it? I'm just trying to process how you can get such a high-resolution understanding of something so chaotic, you know?

speaker: lao
text: The kelp does tell ye somethin', lad, but it's the way the water breaks near the reef that matters most. I've seen the ocean turn spiteful, a greed you can't measure with any gadget you've got. It reminds me of Billy that night, the water just took him clean down where the teeth bite. Now, haul on this last bit, boy, before the tide turns rough again.

speaker: minh
text: Honestly, Jack, this whole thing is a proper adrenaline dump, I've never experienced anything this raw, it's wild. If the kelp is the key, are there certain types of growth patterns or colours that indicate a sudden shift in depth or current, like a kind of bio-indicator? Just gotta keep my wits about me, I think.

speaker: lao
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: The boat is safe and they run to Jack's cottage out of the rain. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Right then, let's get this boat hauled up and away from this muck, lad, before the rain turns to a proper deluge. My cottage is just yonder, keep your footing on the stones, boy. I'll put a fire on, and we'll have a cup of tea strong enough to wake the dead. We'll talk of the old times then, when the sea treated us with more respect than she does now.

speaker: minh
text: Right, a cuppa sounds absolutely vital; I'm proper knackered after this, honestly. It's wild, Jack, I've only ever seen weather simulations, never this real deal, it's a bit much for the circuits. Tell me more about how you'd track those deeper currents without any sort of sonar or depth gauge, it's baffling.

speaker: lao
text: You'll learn to read the water with your bones, lad, not some blinking box. I remember the way the tide pulled out that night, dragging bits of wreckage like toys, and you learn to feel the pull in your gut. It’s the way the wake changes, the subtle shift that tells ye what's deep down there, where Billy was pulled. Now, stop starin' at me like that and help me stack these ropes.

speaker: minh
text: Blimey, Jack, I'm trying to absorb all this, it's seriously nuts out here, a total sensory overload. So it’s all about that gut feeling, that intuitive processing power, basically running on pure, unquantifiable data points. I'll get these ropes stacked, promise; I just find the sheer unpredictability of it all kinda mind-blowing.

speaker: lao
text: Just stackin' the ropes will do ye good for now, lad, don't tax yourself with thinking too much. It's seen plenty of bad weather in my time, the sea takes what it wants, nothing more, nothing less. It reminds me of the sheer bite of the wind that night, the way it ripped the canvas clean off the trawler. Now heave, boy, before the tide turns and leaves us stranded here.

speaker: minh
text: Yeah, yeah, I'll heave, Jack, I'm trying to keep up, this is proper intense, I’ve never seen anything this dramatic, honestly. It’s like the whole environment is running on some kind of faulty hardware right now. Just hope we can get this gear secured before the whole thing crashes out here.

speaker: lao
text: Mind your back, lad, and heave with the rhythm of the waves, not with your mind. This place has stood against storms that'd make your fancy bits quit working for good measure. I still see Billy sometimes in the spray when the wind whips up like that, lad. Now let's get this last coil tight, for the tide waits for no man.

speaker: minh
text: Honestly, Jack, the sheer volume of raw force out here is genuinely terrifying, it's like the whole system is throwing critical errors everywhere. I'm trying to sync up with whatever rhythm you're using, but this level of uncontrolled input is something my coursework never covered. Just trying to keep my bearings, mate; this is way more intense than any controlled lab environment.

summary: Sam and Jack worked together to haul a boat up the slipway during a severe storm. Jack mentioned losing a man named Tom and another man named Billy in a storm in 1987, while Sam learned that Jack relies on instinct and experience rather than scientific measurement to read the sea.

scene_start: Stormy night, Sam stays at Jack's cottage; they sit by the fire.
beats: Jack toasts kippers for Sam.
Sam finally tells the truth about burnout and the breakup.
Jack talks about his late wife.

speaker: minh
director_note: (Director: next in this scene: Jack toasts kippers for Sam. Steer the conversation there naturally.)
text: Blimey, hearing about Tom and Billy really got me thinking about how much you've seen out there. It's weird comparing that to some of the predictive models we mess with in coding, which are all based on historical data points. Speaking of things that keep you going, are those kippers you're about to toast any good, Jack?

speaker: lao
text: Aye, these kippers are from the haul last week, tasted of salt and good fight, lad. Back when I was a lad myself, out near the Banks, the sea would throw up nets full of cod just by the turn of the tide, not by any chart. Remember that time we were caught in a squall off the Lizard, the waves were bigger than the boat itself, proper fighting stuff. You learn to read the water, boy, not by numbers, but by feelin' it in your bones.

speaker: minh
text: It sounds absolutely brutal out there, Jack; I can only imagine the sheer scale of the weather you've dealt with. It's a different kind of 'read' compared to debugging some complex piece of code, I suppose. So, when you say you read the water by 'feel,' is that something you could maybe break down into observable variables?

speaker: lao
text: Now, lad, you're tryin' to measure the wind like it was a bit of rope you could measure twice. I'll tell ye 'bout the time we were out past Mousehole, the water turned a strange milky colour, like bad tea, and the fish just started running deep as if they smelled somethin' wrong. It wasn't the tide, nor the moon, no, but the way the light bent off it, that told me where to drop the pots. You gotta see it with your own two eyes, boy, not with a book.

text: Honestly, it's like you're describing an undocumented variable in a system—something that only appears when you're *there*.
